title: Model games, and what to do when it goes wrong
outcomes: Predicts the next move at twelve decision points in three real Dragon games and names the turning point of each, with the engine's evaluation before and after
Explains in a sentence per phase what each side is doing in a Yugoslav race and in a quiet Classical game
Names three typical Black slips (a delayed rook, ...d5 mistimed, a capture that opens the g-file) and plays the repair in each
Names three typical White slips (the slow rook move, Bh6 without support, the queen on e2) and finds the repair in each
Reads game counts from our data and says what they do and do not show

steps.text: **The question.** What decided real Dragon games, and how do you repair the typical worse positions? You will step through three games between players rated above 2,500, predict decision points, and name each turning point. Then you meet the usual mistakes of both sides and look for the repair. At the end you will teach it back: what decided each game, one typical mistake per side, and its repair. Capablanca left variations in his own book for the reader to work out; do the same: predict before you press.

steps.text: **Game 3: the quiet game.** Not every Dragon is a pawn race. After the Classical set-up both kings castle short; no one pushes a pawn at the king, and the fight is over space and squares. [H] A quiet game rewards the player who keeps improving pieces; a single inaccurate piece move can then decide it, as a single missed tempo decides a race. Predict the plan of each side at each phase.

steps.text: **What decided game 3.** The position was balanced after twenty quiet moves. [V] Two small errors followed: a bishop move that avoided the trade on e3, and then taking the rook on e1 instead of ...Ra8. Each cost roughly half a pawn or more. steps.prompt: Which phase of which game would you play differently, as White or as Black, and what would you change? Answer in a sentence.

steps.text: **A guess about the swings.** [H] In these three games the swing came from an inaccurate move just before a forcing sequence: a wrong capture, a pawn push, a bishop move. Whether that is general is untested, and tempo counting may or may not matter more than learning patterns. Caution: I chose three games with clear stories from the 2500+ games in our data, so they show examples, not how often each happens. Find a game that contradicts the guess.

steps.prompt: Look back at game 1: the combination on g7 took several moves. Does 'one inaccurate move' or 'a tempo race' describe it better? Say why.

steps.text: **Diagnose before you defend.** Znosko-Borovsky (*The Middle Game in Chess*) advises: find your chief weakness and the opponent's chief threat, then choose a long plan, not a single parry; when you stand worse, defend and win back freedom. Emanuel Lasker (*Common Sense in Chess*, Lecture 9) advises vacating weak points and supporting them when compromised. In the Dragon, ask: whose pawns are nearer the enemy king, which file is open, and which trade removes an attacker?

steps.text: **What the three Black slips have in common.** The first lost time (the rook came late), the second broke with ...d5 when White's bishop already stood on c4, the third opened the g-file for White's rook. [I] The break works while the bishop is on f1 and fails once it has come to c4. [H] A repair on the c-file may be more reliable than one on the long diagonal; four positions are not enough to know. Test it on your own games.

steps.text: **Cross-check with our data** (players 2500+). After Black's eighth move, three ninth moves matter. The bishop to c4: 139 games (White 60 wins, 62 draws, Black 17). Long castling: 217 games (69, 102, 46); only 210 have a recorded Black reply. The g-pawn push: 41 games (21, 15, 5). [V] The bishop games average 2934, so many are engine games: read White's 65% as engine-assisted play. Counts show what was played, not what is stronger.

steps.text:
**Recap.**
- Game 1 turned on two moves, game 2 on a slip and a pawn push, game 3 on two bishop moves. [V]
- [H] In these games one inaccurate move came before a forcing sequence; whether that is general is untested.
- [I] Black's repairs here were trades or quiet moves, and they leave Black worse.
- [I] White's repair was to slow Black's race.
- [H] In the Classical, pieces matter more than a race.
- Check the machine's numbers against the sample size.
